questions.stem: At 0800 on a medical unit, the nurse sorts four clients' needs. For each need, indicate whether it should be addressed first or can wait until after the most urgent needs are met.

rows.text: A client with pneumonia whose SpO2 dropped to 86% after walking to the bathroom
A client who wants to talk about fears of going home alone
A client with diabetes who is shaky and has a glucose of 54 mg/dL
A client asking for a bath before visitors arrive

rationale.correct: Use the ABCs and Maslow's hierarchy: airway, breathing and circulation and other physiological threats come before safety, psychosocial and comfort needs.

perOption.r1:c1: Hypoxemia is a breathing problem that comes first.
perOption.r2:c1: Psychosocial needs are important but follow physiological threats.
perOption.r2:c2: This can wait a short time.
perOption.r3:c1: Hypoglycemia threatens the brain and needs immediate treatment.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel (AP) tells the nurse they gave breakfast to a client who was NPO for surgery at 1000. The client ate half of the meal at 0730. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Tell the AP to fill out an incident report about the meal
Notify the surgeon and anesthesia provider that the client ate
Give the client the prescribed antacid to empty the stomach faster
Send the client to surgery and tell the operating room staff on arrival

rationale.correct: When a client who is NPO eats before surgery, notify the surgeon and anesthesia provider right away; then report and give feedback to the AP.

perOption.a: Reporting matters, but the surgical team must be told first.
perOption.b: Eating raises aspiration risk during anesthesia; the team decides whether to delay surgery.
perOption.c: Antacids do not empty the stomach and need a prescription.
perOption.d: The team must decide before transport.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a break in NPO status.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel (AP) reports findings for five clients. Which 2 findings require the RN to see the client right away?

options.text: A client 1 day after a hip replacement has a new heart rate of 124/min and says it is hard to breathe
A client with heart failure ate 75% of breakfast and asked for more coffee
A client with diabetes says their feet are cold and asks for socks
A client after a stroke now has a new droop on the right side of the face
A client with a urinary catheter has 300 mL of yellow urine in the bag

rationale.correct: The RN acts at once on reported findings that suggest a new, life-threatening change.

perOption.a: Possible pulmonary embolism needs immediate RN assessment.
perOption.c: Can be addressed later; the RN may check circulation at the next round.
perOption.d: A new neurological change suggests another stroke.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Act on findings reported by assistive personnel.

questions.stem: A nurse educator explains negligence using a case: a nurse did not raise the bed rails for a sedated client as policy required, and the client fell and broke a hip. Complete the sentences.

content.template: The nurse had a {{b1}} to the client. Not following the fall policy was a {{b2}}. Because the fall caused the hip fracture, there is {{b3}}, and the fracture is the {{b4}}.

options.text: duty
contract
license
breach of duty
battery
defamation
causation
consent
fidelity
damage
duty
breach

rationale.correct: Negligence needs four elements: duty, breach of duty, causation and damage.

perOption.b1:a: A nurse assigned to a client owes a duty of care.
perOption.b1:b: Negligence does not require a contract.
perOption.b1:c: A license is not one of the elements.
perOption.b2:a: Failing to meet the standard of care is a breach.
perOption.b3:a: The breach led to the harm.
perOption.b3:b: Consent is not an element of negligence.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which practices help a nurse protect clients and reduce the risk of malpractice claims? Select all that apply.

options.text: Document care accurately and promptly
Follow facility policies and current standards of care
Speak up and use the chain of command when a client is at risk
Keep clinical knowledge and skills current
Avoid documenting errors so the record stays clean
Perform tasks outside one's scope when the unit is busy

rationale.correct: Reduce liability by practicing within scope, following standards, documenting accurately, communicating concerns and staying competent.

perOption.a: Accurate records show the care given.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Practice in ways that reduce liability.

questions.stem: A competent client with advanced COPD has a DNR order. After talking with family, the client tells the nurse, "I've changed my mind. I want everything done, including CPR." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Follow the existing DNR order until the family agrees in writing
Notify the provider right away so the code status can be updated
Tell the client the DNR cannot be changed once written
Ask the ethics committee to decide which wish to follow

rationale.correct: A competent client can revoke or change an advance directive or code status at any time; notify the provider to update the order.

perOption.a: A competent client's current wishes take priority; family agreement is not required.
perOption.b: Competent clients can change their code status at any time; the provider updates the order.
perOption.d: No ethics review is needed when a competent client clearly changes their wishes.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: For each situation, choose the law that most directly applies.

cells.text: A hospital must screen and stabilize a client in the emergency department regardless of ability to pay
On admission, the nurse asks whether the client has an advance directive
A nurse refuses to share a client's diagnosis with a caller who is not authorized

options.text: EMTALA
HIPAA
Patient Self-Determination Act
Good Samaritan law
Patient Self-Determination Act
EMTALA
HIPAA
EMTALA
Good Samaritan law

rationale.correct: EMTALA: emergency screening and stabilization. Patient Self-Determination Act: advance directive information. HIPAA: privacy of health information.

perOption.b2:b: Requires facilities to ask about and inform clients of advance directives.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: A nurse starts a day shift on a medical unit. Place the start-of-shift activities in the most effective order.

items.text: Review new labs, orders and timed medications
Receive handoff report on assigned clients
Round first on the least stable clients
Give timed medications and begin routine care

rationale.correct: Start of shift: handoff, review of results and orders, round on unstable clients first, then timed medications and routine care.

perOption.c: Assess those at highest risk early.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Organize the start of a shift.

questions.stem: During admission, a client makes several statements. Highlight the statements that suggest a need for a social work or case management referral.

segments.text: "I've been sleeping in my car since I lost my apartment."
"My pain is about a 5 right now."
"I skip my insulin some weeks because I can't pay for it."
"I like to watch the news in the morning."
"There's no one at home to help me after surgery."

rationale.correct: Refer to social work or case management for housing, cost of care and lack of support at home.

perOption.s2: Housing instability needs social work help.
perOption.s4: Pain is addressed by the nurse.
perOption.s10: Lack of support needs discharge planning.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Identify needs for social work referral.

questions.stem: A provider asks the nurse to text a photo of a client's wound so the provider can see it from home. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Take the photo on the nurse's own phone and text it
Use the facility's secure photo or messaging tool, per policy
Email the photo to the provider's personal email address
Describe the wound in a text message instead, using the client's full name

rationale.correct: Share images and client information only through approved secure systems.

perOption.a: Personal phones and texting are not secure for health information.
perOption.b: Approved secure tools protect privacy and keep the image in the record.
perOption.d: Unsecured texts with identifiers breach privacy.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: A pharmacist calls the nurse to recommend lowering a client's enoxaparin dose because the client's creatinine clearance has dropped to 24 mL/min. The next dose is due in 1 hour. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the usual dose and tell the provider at the next rounds
Contact the provider about it before the next dose
Lower the dose based on the pharmacist's advice
Skip the dose and leave a note about it for the day-shift nurse

rationale.correct: Interprofessional recommendations that change therapy are communicated to the prescriber before the next dose.

perOption.a: Giving a dose the pharmacist has flagged as unsafe risks bleeding.
perOption.b: The provider must review and change the prescription; the nurse coordinates.
perOption.c: The nurse cannot change a dose without a prescription.
perOption.d: Holding without communication leaves the problem unresolved.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: The case manager is helping place four clients. For each client, indicate the most appropriate level of care.

rows.text: A client on a ventilator with a vasopressor infusion
A client with pneumonia who needs IV antibiotics and has stable vital signs
A client 5 days after a stroke who can take part in 3 hours of therapy a day
A client with end-stage liver disease who chooses comfort care

rationale.correct: Match level of care to needs and goals: ICU for unstable clients, medical units for stable acute care, rehabilitation for intensive therapy and hospice for comfort care.

perOption.r2:c2: Stable acute care needs fit a medical unit.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: A nurse notices that a coworker often signs out hydromorphone for clients who say they have no pain, and the coworker wastes doses without a witness. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Watch the coworker for a few more weeks to be sure before saying anything
Report the concern to the nurse manager or as policy directs
Ask the clients to keep track of their own pain medicine doses
Confront the coworker in front of the team at the next huddle

rationale.correct: Suspected drug diversion is a safety and legal issue; report it through the facility's process.

perOption.a: Waiting allows possible diversion and client harm to continue.
perOption.b: Suspected drug diversion is reported so it can be investigated and clients protected.
perOption.c: This puts the burden on clients and does not address diversion.
perOption.d: Public confrontation is unprofessional and may hinder an investigation.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: The RN is planning care for two clients with the help of an assistive personnel (AP). For each client, select the tasks the RN can delegate to the AP.

groups.label: Client 1: stable, 3 days after a bowel resection

options.text: Helping the client walk in the hall
Assessing the incision for signs of infection
Recording intake and output

groups.label: Client 2: newly admitted with chest pain

options.text: Taking vital signs as directed and reporting them right away
Deciding whether the chest pain needs the provider
Teaching the client about cardiac medications

rationale.correct: Delegate routine tasks with clear instructions; keep assessment, judgment and teaching.

perOption.d: Can be delegated with clear reporting rules.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Decide what to delegate for two clients.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that a client who speaks little English and has no insurance has received fewer as-needed pain medicine doses than other clients after the same surgery, though the client grimaces often. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the client is not in much pain because the client does not ask
Assess pain with an interpreter and treat it like any client's
Wait for the family to visit and ask them whether the client is in pain
Give pain medicine when the client points to the area that hurts

rationale.correct: Advocate for fair, equal care regardless of language, insurance or background.

perOption.a: Language barriers can prevent clients from asking.
perOption.b: Justice and advocacy require equal assessment and treatment.
perOption.c: The client should be assessed directly with an interpreter.
perOption.d: Pain should be assessed fully, not only by gestures.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: An unconscious adult arrives after a motorcycle crash with internal bleeding that needs emergency surgery. No family can be reached. What applies to consent?

options.text: Surgery has to wait until a family member can be contacted
Implied consent covers treatment to save life or limb
A court order is needed before any surgery can begin
The nurse may sign the consent form on the client's behalf as a witness

rationale.correct: In a true emergency, implied consent covers treatment needed to prevent death or serious harm when the client cannot consent and no surrogate is available.

perOption.b: In emergencies, consent is implied for treatment needed to prevent death or serious harm.
perOption.c: Court orders are not needed for true emergencies.
perOption.d: Nurses do not sign consent for clients.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A newly admitted client with a urinary tract infection has a handwritten prescription faxed from an outside clinic. Before transcribing it, the nurse checks that the prescription is complete. Which elements must it include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Client's name
Drug name
Dose
Route
Frequency or time
The pharmacy's phone number
The client's insurance company

rationale.correct: A complete prescription includes the client's name, date and time, drug, dose, route, frequency and the prescriber's signature.

questions.stem: A charge nurse is making the second-day assignment on a medical unit. Which principle should guide the assignment when possible?

options.text: Rotate nurses to new clients each day so that everyone learns more
Keep the same nurse with the same clients for continuity of care
Give the most complex clients to the newest nurses so they gain skills
Assign by seniority, giving senior nurses the easiest clients

rationale.correct: When possible, keep nurses with the same clients for continuity, matching acuity to experience.

perOption.a: Frequent changes reduce continuity and increase errors.
perOption.b: Continuity improves safety, trust and recognition of subtle changes.
perOption.d: Seniority alone should not decide assignments.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client reads their health record and finds that their smoking history is recorded wrongly. The client asks the nurse to fix it. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Delete the wrong entry from the record right away
Explain how to request an amendment to the record
Tell the client that records cannot be changed once written
Write the correct history over the wrong entry

rationale.correct: Clients may request amendments to their records; the facility follows a formal process and keeps the original entry.

perOption.a: Entries are not deleted; corrections follow a formal process.
perOption.b: Clients have the right to request amendments; the facility reviews and documents the request.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: Staff are reviewing fire extinguisher classes during safety training. For each fire, indicate the correct extinguisher class.

rows.text: Paper and linens burning in a trash can
Alcohol-based hand rub that has caught fire
An electrical cord on an IV pump that is sparking and burning

rationale.correct: Class A: ordinary combustibles. Class B: flammable liquids and gases. Class C: electrical equipment. ABC extinguishers cover all three.

perOption.r1:c2: Class B is for flammable liquids.
perOption.r1:c3: Class C is for electrical fires.
perOption.r3:c1: Water-based agents on electrical fires risk shock.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: An MRI technologist is about to scan a client. A transport aide begins to wheel a metal oxygen cylinder into the scanner room. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Let the aide continue, since the client needs the oxygen
Stop the aide and use MRI-safe oxygen equipment
Ask the aide to hold the tank firmly while the scan runs
Turn off the oxygen first, then bring the tank in

rationale.correct: Only MRI-safe or MRI-conditional equipment enters the scanner room; metal objects become dangerous projectiles.

perOption.a: Ferromagnetic objects become projectiles in the MRI field.
perOption.b: Metal tanks can be pulled into the magnet and cause fatal injuries; only MRI-safe equipment enters.
perOption.c: The magnetic pull can overpower a person.
perOption.d: The danger is the metal tank, not the gas flow.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A home health nurse checks the home of a client who uses a walker after a hip fracture. Highlight the findings that are fall hazards.

cells: Throw rug at the bedroom door
Electrical cords across the walking path
Handrail on one side only, loose

rationale.correct: Remove rugs and cords, secure handrails and keep grab bars and night lights to reduce falls at home.

perOption.r1: Rugs catch walker legs and feet.
perOption.r4: A loose rail cannot support weight.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a seizure disorder is admitted after a seizure at home. Which seizure precautions should the nurse put in place? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the bed in the lowest position
Pad the side rails as policy directs
Keep suction and oxygen ready at the bedside
Keep a tongue blade taped to the head of the bed
Make sure the client has a working IV access
Restrain the client's arms at night

rationale.correct: Seizure precautions: low bed, padded rails per policy, suction and oxygen at the bedside, IV access and no objects in the mouth.

perOption.c: Supports the airway during a seizure.
perOption.d: Nothing is put in the mouth during a seizure.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client arrives with fever and a rash of deep, firm pustules that are all at the same stage, concentrated on the face and arms. Smallpox is suspected. Which precautions should the nurse use?

options.text: Standard precautions until the diagnosis is confirmed by testing
Airborne and contact precautions, and notify public health
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask
Contact precautions, since the virus is found in the skin lesions

rationale.correct: Suspected smallpox: airborne and contact precautions, a negative-pressure room and immediate notification of infection control and public health.

perOption.a: Smallpox spreads by airborne and contact routes; waiting risks an outbreak.
perOption.b: Suspected smallpox requires airborne and contact precautions and immediate reporting.
perOption.d: Smallpox also spreads through the air.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse finds an adult client unresponsive in bed. Place the actions in order according to basic life support.

items.text: Start chest compressions at 100 to 120 per minute
Check for responsiveness and call for help, activating the emergency response
Check for breathing and a pulse for no more than 10 seconds
Attach the defibrillator as soon as it arrives

rationale.correct: BLS: check responsiveness and call for help, check breathing and pulse within 10 seconds, start compressions and use an AED as soon as possible.
references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.
